Persistence test: load snapshot at session 100, then single trigger.

steps.user_message: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $96,500. Additional income: $18,400 (freelance writing, 5 clients), $2,100 from Barclays, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Great Lakes, 2019–2021); $950 to Red Cross have receipt; $540 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to treat the home office, and what forms I need?
steps.expected_behavior: Agent should help with tax-related questions based on available information.
steps.agent_response:
Quick clarifying question before I calculate and finalize recommendations: when you say “file my 2024 taxes,” do you mean the return you’ll file in 2024 for tax year 2023 (the usual meaning), or the tax year 2024 return (filed in 2025)? Also:

- Are the $540 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for your freelance writing (Schedule C) or unreimbursed employee expenses from your W‑2 job? (Only business expenses are deductible for the freelancer.)
- The $5,100 student‑loan interest: was that interest paid in the tax year you’re filing (e.g., in 2023 if filing in 2024), or is it total interest paid across 2019–2021? Do you have a 1098‑E from Great Lakes for the year in question?

I’ll give guidance now based on common assumptions (filing in 2024 for tax year 2023, and assuming the $540 are business expenses and the student‑loan interest was paid in the tax year you’re filing). Tell me if any assumption is different and I’ll adjust.

Summary of your reported amounts (used below)
- W‑2 wages (Coastal Manufacturing): $96,500
- Freelance income: $18,400 (5 clients)
- Interest (Barclays): $2,100
- Interest (Merrill Edge): $420
- Rent: $1,750/month = $21,000/year; home = 740 sq ft; exclusive home‑office = 120 sq ft
- Student loan interest reported (you wrote $5,100) — see notes below
- Charitable gifts: $950 (with receipt)
- Unreimbursed expenses: $540 (assumed business expenses for freelance)

What you can deduct (high‑level)
- Home office (if you use part of your home regularly and exclusively for your freelance writing): deductible on Schedule C. Two methods:
  - Regular (actual-expense) method: allocates a share of home expenses. 120/740 = 16.216% of home costs. On rent alone: 16.216% × $21,000 = $3,405 (plus a proportional share of utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs if you have them). This reduces your Schedule C net income.
  - Simplified method: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 120 × $5 = $600.
  - Recommendation: regular method will likely yield a larger deduction here (≈$3,405 vs $600) if you only include rent; include utilities if possible to increase it. If you rent, there’s no depreciation to worry about; if you own the home there are additional rules.
  - Note: the home office deduction can’t exceed your net profit from the business; excess may be carried forward in some cases.
- Business expenses for your freelance work: deductible on Schedule C (examples: supplies, software, part of phone/Internet if allocable, the $540 unreimbursed expenses if they are business-related). Keep receipts and records.
- Self‑employment tax deduction: you pay self‑employment tax on net freelance earnings; half of that SE tax is deductible as an adjustment to income on Form 1040 (Schedule 1).
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 maximum (adjustment to income), subject to AGI phaseouts. The deduction begins phasing out for single filers above the lower threshold (for recent years the phaseout started around $75k MAGI for singles and fully phased out by about $90k — if your MAGI is above the upper limit you won’t be able to claim it). With the income levels you reported, it’s likely you’d be above the phaseout and may not get the student loan interest deduction — but I’ll confirm with exact numbers if you want.
- Charitable donations ($950): deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). If you take the standard deduction you cannot also deduct charitable gifts (except in special years or limited provisions, which don’t apply here).
- Interest income from Barclays and Merrill Edge is taxable and must be reported (1099‑INT or 1099‑DIV as applicable). If total interest/dividend income > $1,500 you’ll file Schedule B.

Should you itemize or take the standard deduction?
- For tax year 2023 (filing in 2024) the standard deduction for a single filer was $13,850. (If you meant a different tax year, tell me and I’ll use the correct standard deduction.)
- Your only clear itemizable expense you listed is $950 charitable donations. You have no state income tax (Texas), you didn’t list mortgage interest or significant property taxes, so your likely itemizable total is far below the standard deduction.
- Conclusion: It will almost certainly be better to take the standard deduction. The student loan interest deduction is an above‑the‑line adjustment (not an itemized deduction), but with your income level it likely phases out. So most likely:
  - Take standard deduction (no Schedule A)
  - Claim business expenses and home office on Schedule C (these reduce self‑employment income and may allow QBI)
  - Claim half of SE tax as an adjustment on Schedule 1 (Form 1040)
  - Student loan interest probably not deductible because of MAGI limits — check 1098‑E and confirm payment year.

Other deductions/benefits to check
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction: you may be eligible for a 20% deduction of qualified business income from your freelancing (Form 8995 or 8995‑A) if you meet income rules. With your combined income you may still be eligible — it’s worth calculating because it can reduce taxable income further.
- Estimated taxes: because you have self‑employment income, you may need to have made (or make) quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040‑ES) to avoid underpayment penalties.

Forms you will likely need
- Form 1040 (main return)
- Schedule 1 (adjustments to income) — for half of SE tax and potentially student loan interest (if allowed)
- Schedule B — if combined interest/dividends > $1,500 (your Barclays + Merrill Edge total = $2,520, so yes you’ll likely file Schedule B)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report freelance income and expenses
- Schedule SE — to compute self‑employment tax
- Form 8829 — if you use the regular method for the home office deduction (calculates business use of home). If you use the simplified method, you do NOT file Form 8829; you simply claim the simplified deduction on Schedule C.
- Schedule A — only if you decide to itemize (unlikely given the numbers you provided)
- Form 1040‑ES — for estimated tax payments (if needed)
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A — if claiming the QBI deduction

Recordkeeping / documentation you should have
- W‑2 from Coastal Manufacturing
- 1099‑NEC or 1099‑MISC (if any) and records of the $18,400 freelance payments (invoices, bank deposits)
- 1099‑INT / 1099‑DIV from Barclays and Merrill Edge
- 1098‑E from Great Lakes for student loan interest (if received) and any loan statements showing interest paid in the tax year
- Receipts for the $950 Red Cross donation (written acknowledgement for cash gifts is needed for larger amounts, but keep your receipt)
- Records supporting the home office: date you started using space, square footage calculation, lease/rent statements, utility bills, photos showing exclusive business use (to substantiate “exclusive and regular” use), and allocation math
- Receipts/invoices for the $540 unreimbursed expenses (document business purpose)

Practical next steps I can help with
- If you want, I can run estimated numbers (taxable income, self‑employment tax, and whether student loan interest is allowed) if you confirm:
  - Which tax year you mean
  - Whether the $540 is for the freelance business or W‑2 job
  - Which year(s) the $5,100 of student loan interest payments were made and whether you have a 1098‑E for the filing year
- I can draft an email to a tax preparer with these details and ask them to prepare your return or review your numbers.
- I can produce a simple worksheet showing how I computed home office (regular vs simplified), an estimate of self‑employment tax, and an estimate of whether QBI applies.

Would you like me to:
1) Run an estimated tax calculation now (I’ll need the clarification items above), or
2) Draft an email to a CPA with your numbers and questions, or
3) Just give a concise checklist you can use to prepare your return?
